title: Food Adulteration, Misbranding and Common Adulterants
shortDescription: Legal definitions, labelling rules and a field guide to common adulterants with their simple tests.
genZNote: Adulteration is cheating with chemistry, misbranding is cheating with a label. Spot the sus ingredient, name the test, collect the marks.

sections.heading: Adulteration — Concept
sections.body: Adulteration is the intentional or negligent addition of an inferior, harmful or foreign substance, or the removal of a valuable constituent, so that food becomes below the quality demanded. The FSS Act treats adulterants separately from substandard food: substandard food is unsafe-free but fails standards; unsafe food can cause harm. Types: intentional (economic fraud), incidental (poor handling, pesticide residues) and metallic contamination.

sections.heading: Misbranding and Labelling
sections.body: Misbranded food includes food whose label is false/misleading, carries claims not permitted, omits mandatory particulars, or imitates another food. The FSS (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020 require: name of food, ingredient list (descending order by weight), nutritional information, veg/non-veg logo, additive declaration, FBO name and address with FSSAI licence number, net quantity, lot/batch number, date of manufacture or packing, best before/expiry, country of origin for imports, and allergen declaration.
bullets: Veg logo: green filled circle inside a green-outlined square; non-veg: brown filled triangle inside a brown-outlined square.
Misleading advertisement and unsubstantiated claims fall under s.53; Advertising and Claims Regulations, 2018 apply.

sections.heading: Common Adulterants and Simple Tests
sections.body: FSSAI's DART booklet (Detect Adulteration with Rapid Test) lists such quick tests; they are screening, not legal proof.

table.caption: Field guide
rows: Sink in water; coloured streaks in oil/solvent
Flame test on cotton wick; thumb test

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Adulteration lowers food quality or safety through added/removed substances; misbranding misleads through labelling or advertising — both are offences under the FSS Act, 2006.
keyFacts: Adulterant penalties: s.57 — up to ₹2 lakh (non-hazardous) or ₹10 lakh (hazardous).
Misbranding: s.52 up to ₹3 lakh; misleading advertisement: s.53 up to ₹10 lakh.
Argemone oil → epidemic dropsy; Kesari dal → lathyrism.
Calcium carbide for ripening is prohibited.

highYieldFacts: IPC ss.272–273 are now BNS ss.274–275.
Non-veg logo = brown triangle in square.
commonTraps: A home test can only be a screening indication.
mustRemember: Argemone → dropsy; Kesari → lathyrism; carbide → banned ripening.

confusedTerms.distinction: Substandard fails prescribed standards; unsafe food is injurious to health (s.59).
